title: Epistulae
author: Ennodius

passages.original: Exigat licet amor quod non potest implere perfectio et inpetret caritas, ut per loquelae audaciam quae ornare poterat pereat spes tacendi, maxime cum sit dicendi, ut Tullius refert, nisi cum necessaria nimis inepta condicio: sed inter narrationum uias et itinera aperienda falce doctrinae teneri nescius uirium consideratione regnat adfectus. inperatoris loco dominatur semel penetralibus cordis infixa dilectio, credens quod non de uerborum pondere uel pompa capiatur qui de absentis propinqui est salute sollicitus nec existimat quod nasci possit offensa de gratia, hoc ad laetitiam satis esse coniciens, si optatam nuntiet epistula sospitatem.
passages.english: Love may demand what perfection cannot fulfil, and affection may prevail so far that, through the boldness of speech, the hope of silence, which could have adorned [me], perishes, especially since the condition of speaking, as Tully says, is exceedingly inept except when it is necessary. But among the paths of narration and the routes to be opened by the sickle of learning, affection reigns, unable to be restrained by any consideration of its own strength. Love, once fixed in the inner chambers of the heart, rules in the place of a commander, believing that one who is anxious for the welfare of an absent kinsman is not captivated by the weight or pomp of words, nor does he think that offence can arise from kindness, judging this enough for joy, if a letter announces the hoped-for safety.
passages.notes: 'quae ornare poterat' is obscure; it is taken here as referring to silence (the hope of keeping silent, which could have been an adornment). 'Tullius' is Cicero; the reference is not identified here. 'nescius ... teneri' is rendered as 'unable to be restrained'. The syntax of 'nisi cum necessaria nimis inepta' is uncertain: it is taken as 'speaking is exceedingly inept except when it is necessary'.
